content: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by abnormal and excessive electrical activity in the brain's cortical nerve cells, leading to seizures. Despite the introduction of over 10 new antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) since the early 2000s, approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy remain resistant to pharmacological treatment. These patients often require a combination of AEDs to manage their condition. Rufinamide, a novel anticonvulsant medication and a triazole derivative, is structurally distinct from other anticonvulsants currently in use. It was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in January 2009 for the treatment of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in children aged four years and older. Additionally, it is approved as an add-on therapy for adolescents and adults with focal seizures. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of rufinamide as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy. The review included randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving participants of any age or gender with drug-resistant epilepsy. The primary outcome was a reduction in seizure frequency by 50% or more, while secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal, and adverse effects. Data were analyzed using an intention-to-treat approach, and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The overall certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Six trials involving 1,759 participants were included in the review. Four trials (1,563 participants) focused on individuals with uncontrolled focal seizures, while two trials (196 participants) included those with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. The age range of adult participants was 18 to 80 years, and for children, it was 4 to 16 years. The baseline phases of the trials lasted between 28 and 56 days, and the double-blind phases ranged from 84 to 96 days. Five of the six trials adequately concealed randomization, and three trials adequately blinded participants and investigators. Five studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while one study had an unclear risk due to insufficient reporting of study design details. All trials were funded by the manufacturer of rufinamide, introducing a high risk of funding bias. The pooled analysis demonstrated that rufinamide, when added to conventional AEDs, was significantly more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency by at least 50% in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy (RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.22; moderate-certainty evidence). However, data on seizure freedom were limited, with only one study (73 participants) reporting this outcome (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.36 to 4.86; moderate-certainty evidence). Rufinamide was significantly more likely to be withdrawn from treatment compared to placebo (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.45 to 2.31; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse effects were more common in the rufinamide-treated group. The following adverse events were significantly associated with rufinamide use: Headache (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.69; high-certainty evidence) Dizziness (RR 2.52, 95% CI 1.90 to 3.34; moderate-certainty evidence) Somnolence (RR 1.94, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.61; moderate-certainty evidence) Vomiting (RR 2.95, 95% CI 1.80 to 4.82; low-certainty evidence) Nausea (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.64; moderate-certainty evidence) Fatigue (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.97; moderate-certainty evidence) Diplopia (RR 4.60, 95% CI 2.53 to 8.38; low-certainty evidence) There was no significant heterogeneity between studies for any of the outcomes. However, the overall certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate to low due to wide confidence intervals and potential biases in some studies. In conclusion, rufinamide, when used as an add-on therapy, was effective in reducing seizure frequency in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the trials were of relatively short duration, and there is no evidence to support its long-term use. Rufinamide was associated with several adverse effects in the short term. The findings of this review are specific to drug-resistant focal epilepsy and cannot be generalized to other types of epilepsy or to the use of rufinamide as monotherapy.
